baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Connects military history to the domestic politics of wartime government and the politics of high command.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Author’s written answer to “Why did you choose to focus so much of your work on Canada’s role in the world wars?” (2019). This is his research emphasis, not an endorsement of every military or political judgment in the interview.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Makes the disputed charge that specialization and ideological commitments have displaced national history.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: As characterized and challenged in A. B. McKillop’s 1999 abstract, already read in the graph. The polemic itself remains unread. This arrow identifies a contested intervention, not proof of its diagnosis or a general rejection of social history.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: War policy, conscription and the state
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Stacey's official history of war policy (1970) and Granatstein's histories of the King government at war (1975) and of conscription (with Hitsman, 1977) sit between political and military history. Metadata-level only: no abstract or contents page was read for these books. PhD context: 142 of 242 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with Political, international & national history also engage the Canadian military history anchor set (59% vs 14% of all; lift 4.16). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Stacey’s Arms, Men and Governments: The War Policies of Canada (1970) and Morton’s Canada and War: A Military and Political History (1981) join military to political history; Granatstein anchors both entries. Title-level.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The fragmentation charge against the new social history
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Bliss (abstract): twenty-five years of "intense … specialization" replaced older historians' concern for explaining the country. Granatstein, as McKillop summarizes him, accused academic historians of abandoning the national past for "overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history". Cook (2000, abstract) identifies the target as the social history that flowered from limited identities. The critique is from the debate's national side; the replies follow as separate critiques. Scoped to Canadian social history; if Canadian working-class history and Canadian women's & gender history are accepted they carry the specific replies.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Labour historians answer the fragmentation charge
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Two phases. Gregory Kealey answered Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' in the 1992 Journal of Canadian Studies 'Point-Counterpoint', titled "Class in English-Canadian Historical Writing: Neither Privatizing, Nor Sundering"; Palmer's "Of Silences and Trenches: A Dissident View of Granatstein's Meaning" (CHR 80:4, 1999) answers Granatstein's 1998 book. Title and metadata only: neither text was read. PhD context: 22 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Canadian working-class history anchor set (65% vs 22% of all; lift 2.96). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Women's and gender historians answer the lament for national history
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Linda Kealey, Ruth Pierson, Joan Sangster and Veronica Strong-Boag, "Whose 'National' History Are We Lamenting?" (JCS 1992, title), part of the Point-Counterpoint answering Bliss, not Granatstein. Strong-Boag's 1994 address (abstract): "Neo-conservative laments about the state of Canadian history abound"; the old history's "preoccupation with white male elites" and neglect of women and gender, "race" and class show "a restricted vision". She also reviewed Granatstein's book (1999; unread). PhD context: 19 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Canadian women's & gender history anchor set (56% vs 25% of all; lift 2.22). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: National-political history as one side of the debate
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Contesting Clio's Craft (description) names "the political vs. social history debates that have dominated the field since the 1970s". McKay (2000) calls it the "socio-cultural versus national-political impasse". Bliss and Granatstein are political and business historians (see Political, international & national history). Comparison: not every political historian took Granatstein's side. PhD context: 24 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Political, international & national history anchor set (71% vs 19% of all; lift 3.8). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Parallel debates over national narrative in English Canada and Quebec
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Dumont's review of Who Killed Canadian History? (CHA Bulletin 1999, read in full) joins the two debates: she corrects Granatstein's claims about Quebec schooling, calls his book a fierce indictment of social historians with 'visées politiques', and cites Ferretti's chapter in Comeau and Dionne, eds., À propos de l'histoire nationale (1998), and Létourneau's student surveys. Dionne, who reviewed the book in RHAF (1998; title level), co-edited that volume. Létourneau (CHR 2000, abstract) proposes a narration of Canada that is neither unitarist nor fragmenting. Comparison: concurrent, separate debates with limited, one-way textual engagement (Dumont's 1999 review cites Ferretti and Létourneau); no checked Quebec-debate text cites Bliss or Granatstein, and only 4 strict 2009–2026 PhDs cite texts from both. PhD context: 14 of 34 2009–2026 PhDs citing a core debate text also engage the Quebec historiography anchor set (41% vs 16% of all; lift 2.63). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Two 1990s disputes over what historians owe facts and publics
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: McKillop (1999, abstract) answers Granatstein that "event-driven facts are inseparable from considerations of value and therefore from the realm of the interpretive". Comparison only: the Canadian debate was about national history and specialization, not postmodernism; no checked text links it to Jenkins, Evans or Appleby, Hunt and Jacob.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: An intellectual historian criticizes Granatstein's national history
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: McKillop argues that Granatstein "miscasts the role of the scholar as citizen" and that his narrow national history is itself political legitimation. A critique of Granatstein's position within the debate by one intellectual historian, not the whole field's position.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Offers a way past the social versus national-political impasse
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: McKay's abstract frames the prospectus as a way past "the present socio-cultural versus national-political impasse in Canadian history writing"; Ajzenstat sets it against Granatstein's attempt to revive national history. An intervention in the debate's terms, not a party to every exchange in it.

Armstrong (1937), Granatstein and Hitsman (1977), Gagnon (1986, 1995) and Pariseau (1987) write conscription and French-Canadian participation; Gagnon’s 1995 essay assesses French-Canadian historians’ treatment of the Second World War in a Bulletin d’histoire politique dossier on ‘myths and realities’. Overlapping subject and venues, different questions. PhD context: 53 PhDs engage both rosters (expected 26.9).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians': class, ethnicity and gender as what Canadians share, and identities as contingent and multiple (1993–2000)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Cook's own words. 'The New History of Atlantic Canada' (Acadiensis 23:1, Autumn 1993, pp. 146–152, read in full) came between Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) and Granatstein's book (1998): 'one of the sweet ironies in the arid debate between “nationalists” and “limited identitarians” on historiography is that neither side appears to recognize that class, ethnicity and gender describe what groups of Canadians have in common, while “nationalism” most often provokes divisions — “regionalism”!' (p. 146). He holds that 'for all the emphasis on differences during recent decades, Canadians from all regions and linguistic groups have, in fact, been growing more alike, at least in aspiration if not in reality' (p. 146). His 2000 CHR forum essay (pp. 260–265 per Buckner's n. 15) is read only in its abstract: the 'limited identities' hypothesis 'has played a major role in the flowering of social history whose dominance is now being called into question by proponents of a renewed “national” approach'; the debate ignores 'the easy assumption that identities, limited or national, are essential rather than contingent', and 'it is too often forgotten that identities are multiple rather than single'. Context: Bliss's abstract (1991–92) asks historians to remember 'that their subject, after all, is Canada' and does not name Cook. Buckner (2000) writes that Cook in 1995 called the phrase 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8; Canada, Quebec and the Uses of Nationalism, 2nd ed., p. 230, unread here). Buckner then groups Bliss, Granatstein and Owram with Careless's later view that the search for limited identities had 'gone too far' (p. 9). A contribution: Cook is a root of the debate (edge 1) and a respondent who in 1993 placed himself outside both camps.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Cook's phrase 'limited identities' made a programme for Canadian history (1969), and region read through the metropolitan systems that structure it (1979–89)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1969 article (CHR 50:1, pp. 1–10) is unread here; its wording comes from two witnesses. Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, p. 4, read): Careless 'insisted that the “Canadian experience” must be “discerned and defined” through the “limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook”', and concluded that 'the whole may indeed be greater than the sum of its parts, producing through its internal relationships some sort of common Canadianism'. Careless himself, in 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; a lecture given in 1979; read in full, web text without page numbers), summarises the article as noting that these identities 'had tended to bulk larger for Canadians in their history than any identification with overall national patterns of values and attitudes', and quotes its p. 10: 'by pursuing a line largely of sociocultural inquiry, one may hope to uncover satisfactions in the limited identities ... which have added up to some positive balance of satisfaction with Canada itself'. The phrase is Cook's: Careless wrote that he 'did not invent the term “limited identity”, but acquired it from an article by Ramsay Cook, cited in my own article — which was thus essentially a commentary on his initial idea' (1981, n. 1); Buckner (p. 4) says Cook 'coined' it and Careless 'popularized' it. This edge carries Careless's programme, not the coinage. The 1981 lecture joins it to metropolitanism: regionalist historians often present 'an over-simple dichotomy' between a metropolitan central Canada and their own region, whereas 'regions are structured into metropolitan systems both within and beyond their territories'; 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism. Each is inherent in the other'. Frontier and Metropolis (1989) is unread; Rick Szostak's review (Journal of Economic History 50:2, 1990, pp. 499–501, read) reports that in it 'Cities become the foci of regional identity' and that Atlantic Canada 'develops a regional identity despite having no one dominant metropolis' (p. 500). In-period reception: the 1973 bibliography by Hann, Kealey, Kealey and Warrian opened with 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for ... a historical appreciation of the varieties of “limited identities” that constitute Canada' (as Careless quotes it in 1981; a quoted-in witness). Criticism: Buckner (2000, p. 10) answers critics who treat regional studies as, 'as Careless and Granatstein seem to believe, a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state'; Robert Irwin (Journal of Canadian Studies 32:3, 1997; abstract only) argues that prairie identity 'must be understood as an autonomous layer of consciousness rather than a “limited identity” within a national consciousness'; Szostak found the book 'descriptive rather than analytical' and expected readers to be 'left unconvinced' (p. 500). Buckner (p. 5) also notes the different motives: Cook and Careless embraced the concept partly in response to Quebec separatism, Atlantic historians for other reasons. edge_805 and edge_814 stay as group-level arrows.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Limited identities and his own early warning against particularism (1969, 1979–81) as the ground of the later fragmentation debate
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (lecture of 1979, Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; read in full, web text). Ten years after 1969 he sees 'a massive outpouring' of writing on regional interests, cultural discords and class disparities in which 'national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted', and says: 'I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood, when he declared “Lord, I know I prayed for rain — but this is ridiculous.”' He disclaims responsibility for the flood ('I scarcely caused the flood') and does not withdraw the concept: 'I do feel the concept has had much value, and still has'. But 'Unity in diversity' now seems rather 'diversity Unlimited', and 'limited identities remain crucial subjects for the historian's regard — but they should not limit his own perception'; 'Now the task is to cut the sight-lines through'. In-period readings: John G. Reid (Acadiensis 16:2, 1987) records that during the 1980s 'concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result', an argument made in Canada by Careless (graph verification note; not re-read here). Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, read): Careless 'too had come to the conclusion that the search for limited identities had gone too far and threatened the very existence of the Canadian nation-state' (pp. 8–9, citing this lecture); 'More recently the same point has been made, somewhat crudely, by Michael Bliss and Jack Granatstein and with greater sophistication by Doug Owram' (p. 9). Buckner contests the premise, calling the 'so-called fragmentation of the historical profession' 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8). An influence as precursor, not participation: his texts predate the 1991–99 exchanges, and no debate text read here names him except Buckner's. Bliss's 1991–92 article (abstract only) does not name him; Bliss is not presented as answering him. edge_814 (cdn_regional → who_killed_debate) stays: it records regional history as the debate's ground.
